title: Generative Drive Coach
description: UX case study: I was the UX engineer behind Generative Drive Coach, a voice-first AI driving coach at Woven by Toyota, and owned it from research through HMI design and validation.
hmw: help new drivers build real confidence behind the wheel, with voice-first coaching that adapts in real time to parking, intersections, and lane changes?

items.title: My role
items.condensed: UX engineer, Nov 2025 to Oct 2026. I owned research, HMI and voice design, prototyping and validation.

source.text: UX engineer on Generative Drive Coach at Woven by Toyota, November 2025 to October 2026. I owned the experience end to end: research, HMI and voice interaction design, prototyping, and validation.

items.title: Who I worked with
items.condensed: I worked with AI/ML, integration and analyst teams across Woven, TRI, TMNA and TCNA, on CARLA, the Vehicle SDK and CAN signals.

source.text: With AI/ML engineers, systems integration engineers and data analysts across Woven, TRI, TMNA and TCNA. I grounded every design decision in their engineering stack:

items: CARLA: Woven’s proprietary driving simulator, used to test coaching logic before real-world validation.
Vehicle SDK: real steering, speed and sensor signals piped into working prototypes.
CAN signals: live vehicle bus data that tied HMI behavior to actual driving state.

items.title: Prototype ladder
items.condensed: Three fidelities, fastest first: voice-enabled Figma flows, CARLA scenarios, then a physical steering and pedal rig.

source.text: I turned feedback into working prototypes at three fidelities:

items: Voice-enabled Figma flows: fast, low-fidelity concept testing.
CARLA simulator scenarios: realistic, repeatable driving conditions.
Physical steering and pedal rig: paired with updated HUD concepts for hands-on validation.

items.title: Studies I ran
items.condensed: I sorted agency research on 100+ drivers into 22 scenarios, then ran a 25-person simulator study, a 35-participant voice-frequency study and a real-car retest.

source.text: I planned and ran the studies myself, start to finish:

items: Agency research on 100+ drivers, sorted by me into 22 driving scenarios.
A 25-person CARLA simulator study to validate coaching behavior before road testing.
A voice-frequency study with 35 participants, to tune how often and how loudly the coach speaks.
A real-car retest of the re-timed voice instructions.

blocks.text: Voice timed to the moment, not to a schedule

I designed a voice-first coaching layer that gives real-time, context-aware guidance without adding cognitive load, timed to the moment it is needed: a stop sign, an intersection, a lane change. Voice-frequency studies shaped the interaction model by balancing how often the coach speaks against how much a new driver can absorb behind the wheel.
One teen-driving concept became a reusable system of coaching patterns

One teen-driving concept became a reusable pattern system covering parking, intersections, stop signs, turns, lane changes and speed management.
Every pattern shares the same voice-first coaching logic, so a new driving scenario means composing existing building blocks, not starting over.
A small token system (colors, type, spacing and radii) kept the coaching HMI consistent from early dashboard mockups through CARLA test builds and the physical rig.

image.alt: Color tokens. A restrained palette tuned for daylight glare, night driving, and quick at-a-glance recognition.
Type and spacing scales. A screen-legible type scale, sized and weighted for a quick glance at speed. Consistent spatial rhythm across dashboard, HUD, and mobile companion surfaces.
Corner radius tokens. Rounded surfaces calibrated to feel tactile on a touchscreen, not decorative.

blocks.text: Coaching is grounded in live vehicle signals, not a simulated approximation

I partnered with the software-integration and ML teams to ground the HMI in real vehicle state. Live signals from the Vehicle SDK and CAN bus feed the updated HUD concepts, so guidance stays in sync with actual speed, position and steering input.
Coaching behavior was pressure-tested in CARLA before touching a real vehicle

With the ML and research teams, I connected coaching designs to CARLA, Woven’s proprietary simulation platform, to run realistic driving scenarios and pressure-test coaching behavior before it reached a real vehicle.
Physical controls surfaced timing and tone issues a screen-only prototype missed

Feedback moved fast, so my prototypes did too: voice-enabled Figma flows for early concept tests, full simulator scenarios, and a physical rig with a real steering wheel and pedals.

Physical controls surfaced timing and tone issues a screen-only prototype would never catch. Coaching that feels right in Figma can feel intrusive once your hands are on the wheel.
Four calls that shaped the coach

cards.label: Voice over screen
cards.value: Chose voice coaching over on-screen prompts, because gaze studies showed the screen pulled eyes off the road.

cards.label: Timing by speed
cards.value: Chose to time prompts by speed over a fixed distance, because real-car tests showed fixed-distance prompts reached speeding drivers too late.

cards.label: A quieter coach
cards.value: Chose a less talkative AI over a chattier one, because 80% of 35 participants preferred it.

cards.label: Physical rig
cards.value: Chose to test on a physical steering and pedal rig, not only in Figma, because only the rig surfaced timing and tone problems.

blocks.text: What changed, and what limits the numbers

items: Removed: fixed-distance prompt timing. Kept: voice-first coaching. Added: timing by speed, which the real-car retest backed (70% of drivers understood the instructions, a 50% improvement).
Lesson: a screen-only prototype missed timing and tone problems. The physical rig, and the real-car tests after it, caught them.

Limits: the simulator results come from a 25-person study (40% faster to act on the AI’s guidance with the HMI active) and a 35-participant study (80% preferred a quieter AI). Small samples, so I treat them as signals, not proof.
